title: Erectile Dysfunction Drugs Linked to 85% Higher Risk of Serious Eye Conditions, Study Finds
excerpt: A large epidemiological study from UBC confirms what case reports had long suggested: regular use of Viagra, Cialis, and similar drugs significantly raises the risk of three vision-threatening conditions.
body:
• Regular users of erectile dysfunction medications such as Viagra, Cialis, Levitra, and Stendra face an 85% higher risk of developing serious eye conditions, according to a large epidemiological study published in JAMA Ophthalmology.
  • The study from the University of British Columbia is the first to confirm links between PDE5 inhibitors and three specific conditions: ischemic optic neuropathy, retinal vascular occlusion, and serous retinal detachment.
  • A separate study from Weill Cornell Medicine found sildenafil users had a 54% higher risk of serous retinal detachment specifically, though absolute rates remained low at 0.04% over one year.
  • With roughly 20 million monthly prescriptions written in the U.S. alone, researchers say even a small relative risk increase could affect a significant number of people.

A Risk That Was Hiding in Plain Sight

For years, the link between erectile dysfunction drugs and vision problems existed mainly as anecdotal case reports and drug label warnings. A large-scale study from the University of British Columbia has now put hard numbers behind the concern — and they are striking.

Published in JAMA Ophthalmology, the UBC study found that regular users of phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitors — the drug class that includes sildenafil (Viagra), tadalafil (Cialis), vardenafil (Levitra), and avanafil (Stendra) — were almost twice as likely as non-users to develop one of three serious ocular conditions: ischemic optic neuropathy, retinal vascular occlusion, or serous retinal detachment.

"These are rare conditions, and the risk of developing one remains very low for any individual user. However, the sheer number of prescriptions dispensed each month in the U.S. — about 20 million — means that a significant number of people could be impacted."

— Dr. Mahyar Etminan, University of British Columbia

What the Science Shows

PDE5 inhibitors work by blocking an enzyme that regulates blood flow — primarily to treat erectile dysfunction, but the same enzyme exists in blood vessels throughout the body, including the retina. Researchers have hypothesized that the drugs can alter choroidal blood flow and vascular permeability in the eye, potentially triggering retinal pathology.

The UBC findings were corroborated by a separate study from Weill Cornell Medicine, published in the journal Eye in early 2026. That study examined over 200,000 propensity-matched patients and found sildenafil users had a 54% higher risk of serous retinal detachment compared to non-users. The absolute risk remained low — 0.04% over one year versus 0.02% in the control group — but the relative increase was statistically significant.

Notably, the Weill Cornell study found no increased risk for retinal vascular occlusion or ischemic optic neuropathy with sildenafil specifically, suggesting that different PDE5 inhibitors may carry different risk profiles for different eye conditions.

Known Symptoms, Newly Confirmed Risks

Transient visual side effects of PDE5 inhibitors have been documented since the drugs first hit the market. Users have reported blue-tinged vision, heightened sensitivity to light, and blurred vision — symptoms that typically appear within one to two hours of taking the medication and resolve within a few hours. These effects are dose-dependent, occurring in roughly 3-11% of users at standard doses.

What the new research establishes is that the risks may extend beyond these transient effects to include permanent vision damage. Ischemic optic neuropathy — sometimes called a "stroke of the eye" — can cause sudden, irreversible vision loss. Most documented cases occurred within 24 hours of drug use, frequently upon waking the morning after ingestion.

What Users Should Know

Researchers are not calling for people to stop taking the medications but are urging vigilance. "We don't want to alarm people taking them, but generally speaking, if they experience visual problems or changes in vision, then these drugs may be the culprits, and they should check it out," Dr. Etminan told Medscape.

Men with pre-existing risk factors for eye disease — including those with a small cup-to-disc ratio, hypertension, diabetes, or hyperlipidemia — may face compounded risk. Research from the University of New South Wales has also shown that carriers of mutations for retinal diseases like retinitis pigmentosa, who may have normal vision and be unaware of their genetic status, could be particularly susceptible to sildenafil-related retinal damage.
